title: the fight
hook: Hanuman beats every champion Lanka sends, until one weapon he could escape, and chooses not to

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fight, part one. One tree spared, and from the gateway, I am the servant of Rama. Did you notice what you belong to? Today, Lanka sends its best. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Ravana keeps raising the stakes. After the first wave falls, he sends Jambumali, a fierce warrior. Then seven sons of his ministers, in shining chariots. Then five of his generals. Each time, the same news comes back to the palace: the monkey is still on the gate. Then Ravana sends his own young son, Aksha. And Valmiki pauses the fighting for a moment to let Hanuman look at the boy.
screen: `JAMBUMALI, THE SEVEN, THE FIVE.` → `THEN RAVANA'S YOUNG SON.`

segments.voice: Hanuman admires Aksha. Valmiki tells us so. The boy is brave and skilled, radiant like the young sun, and Hanuman feels reluctant to kill one so young. But Aksha's arrows keep coming, and Hanuman decides that an enemy this strong can't be ignored. He kills him. The epic doesn't hide the cost, and it doesn't hide Hanuman's hesitation either. Now Ravana sends his son Indrajit, whose very name means conqueror of Indra. Their duel is long, and neither can wound the other. So Indrajit reaches for the weapon of Brahma, the Brahmastra, and binds Hanuman with it. Hanuman falls, unable to move. And here is the remarkable part. Hanuman knows this weapon. He knows that, by Brahma's own blessing, it can hold him only for a short while. He could wait it out and break free. He chooses to stay down. Why? Because this is exactly what he wanted: to be brought before Ravana. He lets the weapon hold him, out of respect for Brahma, and because it serves his purpose. Then the rakshasas, not trusting the divine weapon, tie him with ropes and bark, and Valmiki says the Brahmastra releases its hold the moment other bonds are added. Indrajit sees it and despairs; their own soldiers have undone his weapon. But Hanuman keeps playing captive. He lets them drag him through the streets, hitting and jeering, into the hall where Ravana sits on his throne. He's fought his way here. Now he's here, and he's going to talk.
screen: `HANUMAN HESITATES OVER AKSHA.` · `INDRAJIT AND THE BRAHMASTRA.` · `HE CHOOSES TO STAY BOUND.` · then, large: `DRAGGED BEFORE RAVANA'S THRONE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Notice where you feel held in place right now: by a chair, a schedule, an obligation. Instead of pushing against it, let yourself be held for a moment, the way Hanuman lets himself be bound. Rest your weight. Breathe. Ask quietly whether any of what holds you might also be carrying you somewhere you need to go. The bell holds the time.
The fight. Wave after wave, the young Aksha, then Indrajit's Brahmastra, which Hanuman could escape but chooses to let hold him, so he can be brought to Ravana.
Your line: he chooses to stay bound. Today, when you could break free of something, ask first whether staying put serves the bigger purpose. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Hanuman bound by Indrajit's Brahmastra, and choosing to submit so as to meet Ravana, appears in recitations and dance-dramas, and some tell it as an example of strength that knows when to yield.

fork.setup: you're Hanuman, bound by the Brahmastra, and you know it will soon let you go. what do you do?
options: stay bound, so they take you to Ravana.
fork.reveal: Hanuman honors Brahma's weapon and lets it hold him, because being captured is the fastest way to stand before Ravana.

original.note: Sanskrit brahmāstra: brahma, the creator, and astra, a missile or divine weapon.

trapdoor: what you thought: Hanuman was finally beaten by Indrajit.
what it means: he chose to be captured, to reach Ravana.

what a scholar hears: the detail that the Brahmastra lets go when ordinary ropes are added is taken by some devotional readers as a lesson about not mixing trust in a higher power with other supports.
